title: The Relationship Cure
author: John M. Gottman and Joan DeClaire
theme: Every close relationship is built, or slowly worn down, by how we respond to the many small daily attempts people make to connect with us.
summary: John Gottman spent decades watching couples, families and friends interact, and with writer Joan DeClaire he set out a simple idea that reaches well beyond marriage. Strong relationships are not mainly made in grand gestures or big talks. They are made in tiny moments, many times a day, when one person reaches out and the other responds.

Gottman calls these reaching-out moments bids. A bid can be a question, a comment about the weather, a joke, a touch on the arm or a sigh at the end of a long day. Each bid is a quiet request for attention, interest or support.

There are three broad ways to answer. Turning toward means noticing the bid and responding with interest, even briefly. Turning away means ignoring it or staying absorbed in something else. Turning against means replying with irritation or a put-down. Gottman's research found that people in lasting, happy relationships turn toward each other far more often, while repeated turning away quietly drains trust over time.

The book explains why responding is not always easy. People differ in their emotional needs, such as wanting to explore, to nurture, to take charge or to have fun, and those differences can cause misunderstandings. Each of us also carries an emotional heritage from our childhood homes, which shapes how comfortable we are with feelings like sadness or anger.

Gottman encourages readers to sharpen everyday skills: noticing body language, listening without rushing to fix things, and naming feelings gently. He also recommends shared rituals, such as a daily check-in, a family meal or a bedtime chat, that make connecting a habit rather than an accident.

The approach works for spouses, children, siblings, friends and coworkers alike. Its hopeful message is that anyone can strengthen a relationship, starting today, simply by noticing the small bids around them and choosing to turn toward.
takeaway: This week, watch for small bids from your partner, children or parents, such as a comment, question or glance, and each time pause what you are doing and turn toward them with a real response.

questions.q: In The Relationship Cure, what is a 'bid'?
options: A formal request for an apology
Any small attempt to get another person's attention, interest or support
A negotiation over household chores
A promise made during a serious argument
questions.why: Gottman uses 'bid' for everyday reaching-out moments, from a question to a touch or a sigh.

questions.q: According to the book, where are strong relationships mainly built?
options: In rare, dramatic gestures of love
In long annual holidays together
Through expensive gifts on special days
In many small daily moments of responding to each other
questions.why: The book argues that connection grows through frequent small exchanges rather than grand events.

questions.q: Which response does Gottman call 'turning toward'?
options: Noticing a bid and responding with interest
Ignoring a bid while busy with a phone
Answering a bid with sarcasm
Changing the subject to your own concerns
questions.why: Turning toward means acknowledging the bid and engaging, even briefly.

questions.q: A parent stays absorbed in the newspaper when a child says, 'Look at my drawing.' What kind of response is this?
options: Turning toward
Turning against
Turning away
A ritual of connection
questions.why: Ignoring or missing a bid is what the book calls turning away.

questions.q: Replying to a partner's comment with an irritated put-down is an example of:
options: Turning against
Turning toward
Emotional coaching
Turning away
questions.why: Hostile or critical replies to a bid are described as turning against.

questions.q: What did Gottman's research find about people in lasting, happy relationships?
options: They rarely make bids to each other
They avoid all disagreements
They spend every evening together
They turn toward each other's bids far more often
questions.why: Frequent turning toward was a key difference between stable, happy relationships and troubled ones.

questions.q: What does the book mean by a person's 'emotional heritage'?
options: Money or property passed down in a family
The ways feelings were handled in the home they grew up in
Their personality type from a quiz
The friends they made at school
questions.why: Emotional heritage refers to how our childhood families dealt with emotions, which shapes us as adults.

questions.q: Why might two people misunderstand each other's bids, according to the book?
options: Because bids only work in writing
Because only children make bids
Because they have different emotional needs, such as wanting to explore, nurture or have fun
Because bids should always be ignored at work
questions.why: Differing emotional needs can lead people to miss or misread each other's bids.

questions.q: Which is an example of a 'ritual of connection' the book recommends?
options: Checking email during family meals
Keeping conversations strictly to logistics
Saving all talks for a yearly review
A regular daily check-in or bedtime chat
questions.why: Shared routines like check-ins and family meals make connecting a dependable habit.

questions.q: Which relationships does the book say its approach can help?
options: Spouses, children, siblings, friends and coworkers
Only newly married couples
Only business partners
Only relationships between parents and teenagers
questions.why: Gottman applies the idea of bids to all kinds of close relationships, not just marriage.
